summary: Nick Ung (Data Science Manager, 6 years at Lyft) and Akshay Sharma (Senior ML Engineer, 4 years at Lyft) present on building evaluations that matter for Lyft's customer support AI agents, which resolve approximately one-third of all customer issues at massive scale. Their agenda covers the end-to-end evaluation pipeline, offline evaluations, online evaluations, eval hardness, future plans, and a config-driven eval harness. They frame agent development as analogous to traditional ML model development, requiring rigorous offline evaluation before production launch. The pipeline has two phases: development followed by offline evaluation (simulated multi-turn conversations, LLM-as-judge grading, launch gates), and production (online graders, tracing, human-in-the-loop feedback feeding back to dev). They identify three common eval failure reasons: scores not meaningfully gating launches, noisy/generic LLM judges producing unactionable insights, and lack of clear regression-catching mechanisms. Their offline simulator draws inspiration from TauBench (Sierra AI), using LangGraph agents interacting with a user LLM defined by intent, data/world state, and behavioral personas. They fine-tuned an LLM on real Lyft user verbatim to replace overly polite frontier-lab LLMs, producing realistic frustrated users and lowering inflated 90%+ pass rates. They defined Lyft user personas including bypassers, refund seekers, and AI skeptics, inspired by a Microsoft user LLM paper. For LLM-as-judge, they found generic pre-built metrics (DeepEval's tool usage appropriateness, response helpfulness, etc.) unactionable. Instead, they frame evals around binary task success/failure, collaborate with domain experts, and define specific rubrics like an education rubric with explicit pass/fail criteria. They validate judges as binary classifiers: hand-label ~100 examples, split into train/dev/test sets, and score precision and recall against human ground truth. They emphasize criteria drift—evaluation criteria must co-develop with model observations and evolve as new data arrives. They recommend adding statistical rigor with confidence intervals, especially for shipping decisions. An error analysis loop runs continuously: deep-dive raw traces, pinpoint failure modes, keep only decision-changing metrics, form fresh premises, and repeat. Tracing tools like LangSmith and LangFuse capture full graph execution, while annotation queues let domain experts label examples without reading raw JSON. They close with continual learning across three dimensions: model learning (post-training, updating model weights, training custom LLMs), context learning (improving documents, memories, tool outputs the agent receives), and harness learning (updating system prompts, tool schemas, control flow, routing, retries). Looking ahead, they plan to build a systematic, config-driven eval harness stored as YAML files editable by analysts and data scientists, with primitives like task, datasets, personas, LM adapter, and evaluator. This harness enables running evaluations at multiple touch points—local development, pre-commit hooks, and CI/CD regression and acceptance test suites. They also plan to explore post-training and reward modeling for reinforcement learning, leveraging accumulated real user signals.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Offline evaluation should gate production launches for AI agents, just as it does for traditional ML models—never use live users as test data.

Fine-tuning a user LLM on real verbatim and defining user personas (bypasser, refund seeker, AI skeptic) produces realistic adversarial simulations that lower inflated pass rates and surface real failure modes.

Generic pre-built LLM judge metrics (e.g., DeepEval's helpfulness, naturalness) are unactionable; evals should be framed as binary task success/failure tied to business outcomes and co-developed with domain experts.
Validate LLM judges as binary classifiers: hand-label ~100 examples, split into train/dev/test, and measure precision and recall against human ground truth to ensure reliability.
Add statistical rigor (confidence intervals, proper sampling) to reported numbers, especially for shipping decisions; small gains on small sample sizes may not be real.

Close the evaluation loop through continual learning across three dimensions: model learning (post-training, weights), context learning (documents, memories, tool outputs), and harness learning (prompts, tool schemas, control flow, routing).

A systematic, config-driven eval harness with standard primitives (task, datasets, personas, LM adapter, evaluator) enables repeatable evaluation at multiple touch points—local dev, pre-commit hooks, and CI/CD regression suites.
Error analysis loops must run continuously on a regular cadence, not as a one-off audit, feeding identified failure modes back into agent prompt, knowledge, and context management improvements.

sections.title: Speaker Introductions
sections.summary: Nick Ung (Data Science Manager, 6 years at Lyft) and Akshay Sharma (Senior ML Engineer, 4 years at Lyft) introduce themselves and their work on Lyft's customer support AI agent platform.

sections.title: Agenda Overview
sections.summary: The talk covers end-to-end evaluation pipeline, offline evaluations, online evaluations, eval hardness, and future plans for building customer support AI agents.

sections.title: High-Level Evaluation System
sections.summary: Describes the development phase (context, tools, agentic graph, system prompt) followed by offline evaluation (simulated multi-turn conversations, LLM-as-judge, launch gate), then production with online graders, tracing, and human-in-the-loop feedback. Emphasizes not using live users as test data.

sections.title: Three Common Reasons Evaluations Fail
sections.summary: Identifies three failure modes: scores not meaningfully gating launches, noisy/generic LLM judges that produce unactionable insights, and lack of clear regression-catching mechanisms with accountable owners.

sections.title: Offline Evaluation System Design
sections.summary: Details the offline simulator inspired by TauBench from Sierra AI, using LangGraph agents interacting with a user LLM defined by intent, data/world state, and behavioral personas. The grader combines LLM-as-judge with deterministic code assertions for instruction-following accuracy.

sections.title: Synthetic Data Challenges
sections.summary: Explains that simply prompting an LLM to generate test queries is insufficient. Recommends sampling real production data and mutating criteria to cover golden paths and edge cases for representative offline datasets.

sections.title: User Simulator Problem and Solution
sections.summary: Frontier-lab LLMs used as user simulators produce overly polite, verbose queries yielding inflated 90%+ pass rates. Real users are terse and frustrated. Solution: fine-tune an LLM on real Lyft user verbatim to produce realistic, production-matching user behavior.

sections.title: Fine-Tuned User Simulator Benefits and Personas
sections.summary: After fine-tuning, evaluation scores dropped as expected, making evals harder and more realistic. They defined Lyft user personas (bypasser, refund seeker, AI skeptic) to ground the user LLM, inspired by a Microsoft user LLM paper that similarly fine-tunes until scores go down.

sections.title: LLM-as-Judge: From Generic to Actionable Metrics
sections.summary: Generic pre-built metrics like DeepEval's tool usage appropriateness and response helpfulness are not actionable. Akshay advocates framing evals as binary task success/failure, collaborating with domain experts, and aligning metrics with business goals. Example: education rubric with explicit pass/fail criteria for when the agent educates too much or too little.

sections.title: Validating LLM Judges as Binary Classifiers
sections.summary: Treat LLM judges as traditional binary classifiers. Hand-label ~100 examples with pass/fail, split into train/dev/test sets. Use train for few-shot prompt examples, iterate on dev, validate on test to check for overfitting. Score precision and recall against human ground truth.

sections.title: Criteria Drift and Evolving Evaluation
sections.summary: Evaluation criteria cannot be fully defined upfront; they must co-develop with model observations. As more examples are graded, criteria should evolve. The judge prompt and metrics should be refined iteratively.

sections.title: Statistical Rigor for Reported Numbers
sections.summary: Add confidence intervals and proper sampling to reported alignment rates, especially for shipping decisions. Example: 84% vs 88% on 50 samples is insufficient to confirm a real gain. Reserve expensive rigor for high-stakes moments.

sections.title: Eval Anti-Patterns and Data Importance
sections.summary: Lists observed eval anti-patterns including ignoring data, which is foundational. Without looking at data, you cannot create meaningful criteria, labels, or validate judges. Cannot rely on LLMs for everything yet.

sections.title: Continuous Error Analysis Loop
sections.summary: A continuous loop: deep-dive raw traces, pinpoint failure modes, keep only decision-changing metrics, remove noise, form fresh premises, and repeat on a regular cadence (weekly or bi-weekly). Not a one-off audit.

sections.title: Tracing and Annotation Queues
sections.summary: Tracing tools like LangSmith and LangFuse capture full graph execution, nodes, tools, token usage, and latency. Annotation queues provide domain experts an easy UI to label examples and give feedback, forming the basis for ground-truth labels and judge validation.

sections.title: Continual Learning: Model, Context, and Harness
sections.summary: Nick details three continual learning dimensions: model learning (post-training, updating weights, training custom LLMs), context learning (improving documents, memories, tool outputs the agent receives), and harness learning (updating system prompts, tool schemas, control flow, routing, retries). Error analysis insights feed back into agent prompts, knowledge space, and context management strategy.

sections.title: Future Plans: Systematic Eval Harness and Post-Training
sections.summary: Current offline simulator scripts are scattered across notebooks and repos, lacking repeatability. Plans include building a systematic eval harness with standardized primitives and contribution workflows. Also exploring post-training: fine-tuning models for different customer support tasks and framing reward modeling problems for reinforcement learning, leveraging accumulated real user signals.

sections.title: Eval Harness Design and CI/CD Integration
sections.summary: The eval harness is config-driven using YAML files editable by analysts and data scientists, not just engineers. Standard primitives include task, datasets, personas, LM adapter, and evaluator. Supports parallelism for thousands to tens of thousands of examples. Config is defined once and run at multiple touch points: local development for immediate feedback, pre-commit hooks to prevent regressions, and CI/CD for regression and acceptance test suites. Nick and Akshay close by inviting the audience to connect and share evaluation learnings.

demonstrations: Comparison of frontier-lab LLM user verbatim (verbose, polite) versus real Lyft user verbatim (terse, frustrated) to illustrate the simulation gap

Data splitting approach for validating LLM judges: train set for few-shot prompt examples, dev set for prompt iteration, test set for final validation against overfitting
Statistical significance example: two evaluators scoring 84% vs 88% on 50 samples showing that a 4% gain may not be real without more samples
